question: What does “Big Ben” technically refer to?
note: Big Ben is the nickname of the Great Bell, which weighs about 13.7 tonnes and first rang in 1859. It cracked within a few months of going into service, and that crack is what gives the chime its particular tone. The tower was known simply as the Clock Tower until 2012, when it was renamed Elizabeth Tower for the Queen’s Diamond Jubilee.

question: What is the usual nickname for the London Underground?
note: The London Underground opened in 1863 and was the first underground railway in the world. The nickname comes from the deep circular tunnels bored for the later electric lines, and it took hold after newspapers dubbed the Central London Railway the “Twopenny Tube” when it opened in 1900 with a flat fare of two pence.

question: Which English city stands over the only hot springs in Britain?
note: The Romans called the town Aquae Sulis, after Sulis, a local goddess whom they treated as a version of their own Minerva. The hot springs under it still rise at around 46°C and deliver more than a million litres a day.

question: Where is the Giant’s Causeway?
note: The causeway is made of around 40,000 basalt columns, most of them six-sided, left behind when a thick flow of lava cooled and cracked about 60 million years ago. Irish legend explains them another way, telling of the giant Fionn mac Cumhaill laying the stones so he could walk across to Scotland.

question: In which English county is Stonehenge?
note: Stonehenge stands on Salisbury Plain and was built in stages beginning around 3000 BC. Many of its smaller bluestones came from the Preseli Hills in west Wales. The central Altar Stone has a different story, with research published in 2024 tracing its geological origin to north-east Scotland.

question: Loch Ness is in which part of the UK?
note: Loch Ness lies along the Great Glen in the Highlands and stretches about 37 kilometres. It holds more fresh water than every lake in England and Wales combined, and the peat washed into it keeps the water so dark that divers can see very little below the surface.

question: 10 Downing Street is most closely associated with which office?
choices: The Speaker of the House of Commons
note: Robert Walpole moved into Number 10 in September 1735, after the house had been joined to a larger property behind it. He had declined George II’s offer of a personal gift and asked for it to belong to the office of First Lord of the Treasury. Some later prime ministers preferred their own homes, so residence there was far from continuous.

question: Robin Hood is traditionally associated with which forest?
note: Sherwood was a royal hunting forest in Nottinghamshire, but of the four earliest Robin Hood ballads only Robin Hood and the Monk names it; the other three are set around Barnsdale in Yorkshire. The Major Oak, long said to have sheltered the outlaws and thought to be 800 to 1,200 years old, failed to come into leaf in 2026, and the RSPB, which manages the forest, announced that it had died.

question: Which theatre is most closely associated with Shakespeare’s company in London?
note: The Globe opened on the south bank of the Thames in 1599, built from the timbers of an earlier playhouse that the company had dismantled and carried across the river. It burned down in 1613 when a cannon fired during a performance of Henry VIII set the thatched roof alight.

question: The Brown family meet a bear at a London railway station and name him after it. Which station?
note: Michael Bond’s bear is found at Paddington station with a label asking that he be looked after, and the Browns name him for the place where they meet him. Bond gave the bear a home in Peru after he was reminded that there are no bears in Africa, where he had first placed him.

question: Which city is most closely associated with the Beatles’ beginnings?
note: The Beatles came together in Liverpool at the end of the 1950s and played close to 300 shows at the Cavern Club on Mathew Street. Their long residencies in Hamburg in the early 1960s are usually credited with turning them into a hardened live band before they became famous at home.

question: In what year was the Battle of Hastings?
note: The battle was fought on 14 October 1066, a few miles inland from Hastings at the place now called Battle. It ran for most of the day, which was unusually long for medieval fighting, and it ended Anglo-Saxon rule in England.

question: Who defeated Harold II at the Battle of Hastings?
note: William, Duke of Normandy, won at Hastings and was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066. At Christmas 1085 he ordered the survey recorded in Domesday Book, which set down who held what across most of England in such detail that courts were still citing it in the twenty-first century.

question: In which year was Magna Carta first sealed?
note: King John put his seal to Magna Carta at Runnymede in June 1215 under pressure from rebel barons. He had it annulled by the Pope within ten weeks, and the version that became law was reissued after his death. Four copies of the 1215 document survive.

question: The Gunpowder Plot took place in which year?
note: The plotters meant to blow up the House of Lords at the state opening of Parliament on 5 November 1605 and put a Catholic monarch on the throne. An anonymous letter warning one peer to stay away from the opening led to the search that uncovered the cellar.

question: What was Guy Fawkes found guarding beneath the House of Lords?
note: Fawkes was found in a cellar beneath the House of Lords with 36 barrels of gunpowder, enough to have destroyed the building. He had spent years soldiering in the Spanish Netherlands, which is why the group put him in charge of the explosives.

question: Which two houses fought the Wars of the Roses?
note: The houses of Lancaster and York fought for the English throne from 1455 to 1487. The name came into use long afterwards and refers to their red and white rose badges, which Henry VII combined into the Tudor rose once he had taken the crown.

question: How many wives did Henry VIII have?
note: Henry VIII married six times in his search for a male heir who would outlive him. His wives’ fates are remembered by a rhyme: divorced, beheaded, died; divorced, beheaded, survived. The son he finally had, Edward VI, died at fifteen.

question: Who was the mother of Elizabeth I?
note: Elizabeth I was the daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, who was executed when Elizabeth was two years old. Elizabeth was declared illegitimate soon afterwards and reached the throne only in 1558, once both her half-siblings had reigned and died.

question: Which Scottish king became James I of England after Elizabeth I died?
note: James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603, bringing the two crowns together under one king while the countries kept their separate parliaments. He was the son of Mary, Queen of Scots, whom Elizabeth I had ordered executed sixteen years earlier.

question: In what year did the Great Fire of London begin?
note: The fire started in a bakery on Pudding Lane in the early hours of 2 September 1666 and burned for four days. It destroyed some 13,200 houses and the old St Paul’s Cathedral, although the recorded death toll was remarkably small.

question: Which British monarch became Empress of India in 1877?
note: Victoria came to the throne in 1837 at eighteen and reigned until 1901, longer than any British monarch before her. She withdrew from public life for years after Prince Albert died in 1861, and her long mourning shaped much of how the era is now remembered.

question: The people often called “Beefeaters” at the Tower of London are officially known as what?
note: The Yeoman Warders are the ceremonial guardians of the Tower and live within its walls with their families. Their history is linked to the monarch’s Yeomen of the Guard, but the Tower’s warders became a separate body under Henry VIII. The nickname “Beefeater” is commonly connected with their beef rations, although its origin is uncertain.

question: In the medieval romances, whose sword is Excalibur?
note: Excalibur is King Arthur’s sword in the medieval romances, although the stories disagree about where it came from. In some accounts it is the sword he pulls from the stone, and in others the Lady of the Lake hands it to him after that first sword breaks.

question: In the famous story of King Cnut and the tide, what is the king trying to demonstrate?
choices: That the sea belongs to the crown
note: The story comes from Henry of Huntingdon, writing about a century after Cnut died. Cnut had his throne carried to the shore and ordered the tide to halt, and when the water came in anyway he told his courtiers that the power of kings is empty beside God’s. The tale is often retold backwards, as though he had believed the sea would obey him.

question: Bonfire Night is observed on which date?
note: Bonfire Night marks the failure of the Gunpowder Plot on 5 November 1605. In 1606 Parliament made the day an annual public thanksgiving by law, and that act stayed on the statute book until 1859.

question: Boxing Day falls on which date?
note: Boxing Day falls on 26 December, which is also St Stephen’s Day. The name is generally connected with Christmas boxes of money or gifts given to servants and tradespeople, although its precise origin is uncertain. The date also became a major occasion for sporting fixtures in Britain.

question: Pancake Day in Britain is another name for what?
note: Shrove Tuesday is the last day before Lent, and the pancakes exist to use up eggs, butter and other rich food before the fast began. “Shrove” comes from shriving, the old word for confessing and being absolved, which was done on the same day.

question: Who wrote Pride and Prejudice?
note: Pride and Prejudice appeared in 1813, although Austen had written a first version called First Impressions in the 1790s and seen it turned down by a publisher who never read it. All her novels were published anonymously in her lifetime, and her name appeared on them only after her death.

question: Ebenezer Scrooge appears in which Dickens work?
note: Dickens wrote A Christmas Carol in about six weeks in 1843 and paid for the printing himself after falling out with his publishers over money. The first run sold out before Christmas, and “Scrooge” entered English as a word for a miser.

question: Who created Sherlock Holmes?
note: Conan Doyle apparently killed Holmes in “The Final Problem,” published in 1893. The detective appeared again in The Hound of the Baskervilles, serialised in 1901–02, but that story was set before his supposed death. His survival was finally explained in “The Adventure of the Empty House” in 1903.

question: Hercule Poirot was created by whom?
note: Christie introduced Poirot in her first novel in 1920, making him a Belgian refugee of the kind she had seen arriving in her home town during the First World War. She grew tired of him decades before she stopped writing him, and finally killed him off in a book she had kept locked away since the 1940s.

question: Who wrote The Woman in White?
note: The Woman in White ran as a serial in Dickens’s magazine All the Year Round from 1859 and made Collins’s name with the reading public. It helped establish the sensation novel, and shops sold Woman in White bonnets and perfumes on the strength of it.

question: Who wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four?
note: Orwell wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four on the Scottish island of Jura while seriously ill with tuberculosis, and it was published in 1949, seven months before he died. The title is often said to invert 1948, the year he finished the manuscript, but his drafts show that he tried 1980 and 1982 first.

question: Who created James Bond?
note: Fleming wrote Casino Royale at his house in Jamaica in 1952 and took the name from an American ornithologist whose field guide to Caribbean birds sat on his shelf. He had worked in naval intelligence during the war, which supplied much of the material.

question: Who plays Mr Bean?
note: Rowan Atkinson created Mr Bean with Richard Curtis, and the character barely speaks, which let the show travel almost anywhere without translation. Only fourteen half-hour episodes were made between 1990 and 1995.

question: In Doctor Who, what does TARDIS stand for?
choices: Time And Relative Dimension In Space
Travel Across Real Dimensions In Space
Time And Reality Device In Space
Temporal And Relative Distance In Space
note: TARDIS stands for Time And Relative Dimension In Space, a name the Doctor’s granddaughter Susan claims to have made up herself in the very first serial in 1963. The ship is meant to disguise itself wherever it lands, but its camouflage circuit had already failed when the series began, leaving it a 1960s London police box.

question: In which comedy series did the Dead Parrot sketch first appear?
note: Monty Python’s Flying Circus began on the BBC in October 1969, late at night and with almost no promotion. The team often let a sketch drift to a close without a punchline, which broke sharply with the sketch shows around them.

question: Which playwright wrote The Birthday Party and The Caretaker?
note: A Pinter pause is a silence written into the script, where what the characters avoid saying carries the weight of the scene. He marked them so precisely that actors treat his “pause” and his longer “silence” as separate instructions. Pinter won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2005.

question: Doctor Who was first broadcast on the BBC in which decade?
note: The first episode went out on 23 November 1963, the day after President Kennedy was assassinated. The BBC repeated it the following week before showing the second episode. About 4.4 million people watched the original broadcast, while the repeat reached six million, giving the series a larger second audience for its opening.

question: In “bangers and mash,” what are the bangers?
note: Bangers and mash is sausages with mashed potato, usually under onion gravy. The word “banger” is said to come from the First World War, when sausages made under meat rationing held so much water that they burst loudly in the pan.

question: Traditional shepherd’s pie is made with which meat?
note: Shepherd’s pie is made with lamb or mutton, and the same dish made with beef is usually called cottage pie. Cottage pie is the older name, recorded in 1791, and the two names were used for any meat until the split between lamb and beef settled in the twentieth century.

question: Haggis is especially associated with which country?
note: Haggis is sheep offal minced with oatmeal and suet and traditionally cooked inside the animal’s stomach. At a Burns Supper it is carried in behind a piper, and Burns’s “Address to a Haggis” is recited over it before it is cut open.

question: What is inside the sausage-meat coating of a Scotch egg?
note: A Scotch egg is a boiled egg wrapped in sausage meat and breadcrumbs. Fortnum & Mason claims to have invented it in 1738, although the claim is hard to prove and similar dishes existed elsewhere.

question: A traditional cream tea usually includes scones with what?
note: A cream tea is scones with clotted cream and jam, served with a pot of tea. Devon and Cornwall are said to disagree over the order, the Devon method putting the cream on first and the Cornish the jam, although tea rooms in both counties serve it either way.

question: Which of these would be least typical on a full English breakfast?
note: A full English is built around fried or grilled items such as bacon, sausage, eggs, beans, tomato, mushrooms and toast, with black pudding appearing in many regional versions. A croissant belongs to the continental breakfast, which is why it stands out here.

question: Which food is famously associated with spectators at Wimbledon?
note: Strawberries and cream have become part of the Wimbledon experience as firmly as the tennis. The tournament’s fruit has been supplied by Hugh Lowe Farms in Kent, where berries are picked by hand early in the morning and checked before dispatch. Each batch can be traced back to where and when it was picked, and even to the picker.

question: Under the modern Laws of Cricket, how many legal deliveries are in an over?
note: An over is six legal deliveries, and a ball bowled as a no-ball or a wide does not count towards it. The number has moved about over the years, with four-ball and eight-ball overs both in use at different times before six became standard everywhere at the end of the 1970s.

question: The annual Boat Race is traditionally contested by which two universities?
note: The familiar course between Putney and Mortlake was first used for the men’s Boat Race in 1845, although there have been exceptions, including the 2021 race at Ely. It runs about 6.8 kilometres. The crews row upstream with the incoming tide, timing the race to benefit from the current.

question: The Ashes is a cricket series between England and which country?
note: The Ashes name grew from a mock obituary published after Australia beat England at the Oval in 1882, declaring English cricket dead. The small terracotta urn was originally a personal gift to England captain Ivo Bligh. It belongs to the MCC collection at Lord’s and has occasionally travelled on exhibition; the winning team receives a separate trophy.
